text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Tuesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
--- More and more Danes are seeking economic help from private sector aid organisations due to tighter rules for receiving social benefits from state local authorities

--- Denmark's government seems to have cleared the way for the passage through parliament of its 1997 state budget by making concessions on social issues to the left-wing opposition Socialist Peoples Party and Unity List.
--- Use of the extasy drug is still on the increase in Denmark with police confiscating 8,500 pills by end-September, four times more than last year.
--- Denmark's Central Bank unveiled its new 200 crown note to be introduced in March next year. The note is part of a series to replace notes currently in circulation by 1999.
--- More than 50 percent of all Danes work in public or private service companies, but Danish industry is still creating most new jobs, a Danish Confederation of Industry survey shows.

--- The number of service jobs is increasing faster in the provinces than in Copenhagen, according to a survey by Denmark's Statistical Office, giving the lie to the myth that the capital has experienced a service job boom while industrial firms quit the region for western Denmark.
